title: Quantum prepare-and-measure scenarios: concepts and methods
authors: A. de Oliveira Junior, Santiago Zamora, Jonatan Bohr Brask, Rafael Chaves, Armin Tavakoli
abstract: Prepare-and-measure scenarios are among the simplest and most widely used settings for quantum communication. A sender prepares a physical system in one of several possible states, which a receiver then measures. Despite this simple structure, these scenarios offer a rich framework for exploring the differences between classical and quantum communication, revealing quantum advantages, and developing protocols for quantum cryptography and device certification. In this tutorial, we give a ground-up introduction to prepare-and-measure scenarios and the methods used to study them. We introduce different frameworks for constraining and characterising communication, with an emphasis on semi-device-independent approaches to quantum information. We also cover modern convex-optimisation techniques for characterising the correlations achievable in these scenarios and illustrate how these tools can be applied in practice. Our aim is to give newcomers the conceptual and technical foundations needed to approach the current literature and apply prepare-and-measure methods in their own research. We conclude with a discussion of open problems and directions for future work.
summary: This tutorial provides a detailed mathematical and conceptual guide to prepare-and-measure quantum scenarios. It introduces how these simple models are used to quantify quantum advantages over classical limits by characterizing the polytope of achievable correlations. The work heavily relies on advanced tools from convex optimization and linear algebra to provide a rigorous foundation for the field.
main_problem: The paper aims to provide a comprehensive, ground-up introduction to prepare-and-measure (PM) scenarios as a framework for studying quantum advantages over classical communication.
main_result: It establishes that the set of achievable classical correlations in PM scenarios forms a polytope, and it details the use of convex optimization and linear algebra to characterize the boundaries of this polytope.
method: The authors employ convex optimization techniques, specifically formulating the problem as Linear Programs (LPs) and Semidefinite Programs (SDPs), and using combinatorial arguments to prove facet inequalities.
model_or_system: The core model is the Prepare-and-Measure (PM) scenario, where a sender prepares a state and a receiver measures it, defined by input alphabets X and Y, and output B. The analysis focuses on bounding the achievable probability distributions p(b|x, y).
key_observables: The conditional probability distribution p(b|x, y) and the success probability in the communication protocol.
important_parameters: The alphabet sizes (|X|, |Y|, |B|) and the message dimension (d) are key parameters defining the scenario constraints.
main_assumptions: The analysis often assumes the existence of a shared classical random variable ($\lambda$) to model classical correlations, and the optimization framework assumes finite-dimensional problems.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the general structure of PM scenarios and the 'Classical polytope,' showing that classical correlations are the convex hull of deterministic strategies.
paper_structure: The tutorial progresses from motivation to dimension-restricted scenarios (classical models), then covers entanglement-assisted scenarios, alternative assumptions, and concludes with open problems.
why_interesting: While focused on general quantum information theory, the rigorous mathematical tools—convex optimization, duality theory, and polytope characterization—are highly relevant for analyzing resource constraints in open quantum systems or quantum communication protocols.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Schematic representation of a PM scenario. Alice receives an input x ∈{1, ..., |X|} and prepares a message for Bob, possibly assisted by a shared resource R. The communication is subject to a physical constraint, and may be either classical C or quantum Q. Bob then chooses an input y ∈{1, ..., |Y|}, performs his measurement, and produces an output b ∈{1, ..., |B|}.

Figure 2. Classical polytope. Toy illustration of the set of classical correlations in dimension-restricted PM scenarios with shared ran- domness. The set is a polytope characterised by the convex hull of the probability distributions associated with all deterministic encod- ing/decoding strategies for Alice and Bob.

Figure 3. Classical and quantum correlation sets. Schematic illus- tration of the classical set L and the quantum set Q in a PM scenario with shared randomness. The inclusion L ⊆Q follows because clas- sical messages can be represented by quantum states diagonal in a common basis. Whether the inclusion is strict, as illustrated above, ultimately depends on the specific input-output scenario.

Figure 4. Prepare-and-measure networks with quantum messages. (a) Two preparation devices send quantum messages to a single mea- surement device, enabling the certification of whether the receiver performs an entangled measurement. (b) The quantum state prepared by the sender is transmitted through a broadcasting channel to two spatially separated measurement devices, enabling the activation of the nonclassicality of the prepared states.

Figure 5. Lowest-level moment matrix. Illustration of the SDP ma- trix Γ for J = L = {1, {ρx}x, {Mb|y}b,y}. The entries encode normal- isation, purity, projectivity and the probabilities p(b|x, y) = Γρx,Mb|y. Shaded blocks highlight the different structural blocks of the matrix and coloured symbols indicate free parameters subject to these linear constraints.
